1:
The king’s name differs between the two accounts, and is explained two ways. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads a deliberate disgrace: in Chronicles, where no wickedness is laid to his charge, he is Abijah, my father is the Lord, while here, where his faults are told, the name of God is taken from his name. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) thinks the Chronicles form probably correct as the more significant, and the variation here either a false reading or a change made to distinguish him from Jeroboam’s son. On the length of the reign the arithmetic is agreed and the stated figure is not: John Gill (reformed) makes it one whole year and part of two, Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) two years and a few months rather than three full ones. Henry alone gives a reason for it, that being made proud by his great victory the king was cut off to make way for a better son.

The queen mother draws attention for her descent. Henry takes Abishalom for Absalom, David’s son, the more readily because two others of Rehoboam’s wives were his near relations, and remarks that the king thought it below him to marry outside the royal line. Ellicott agrees and adds the complication: elsewhere she is called Michaiah and daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, which with the chronology shows she must have been Absalom’s granddaughter; of eighteen wives and threescore concubines she was the favourite. Keil and Delitzsch meet another difficulty, that the identical notice recurs of the next king’s mother, and refuse the inference that a man had his own mother to wife.

The imperfect heart is taken as idolatry. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says flatly that he was an idolater who did not support the true worship, which he takes to be the general force of the phrase. Ellicott infers from its qualified wording that, like Solomon and Rehoboam, the king worshipped Jehovah only as the supreme God of his pantheon, and calls it a curious irony that he should be recorded inveighing against the degradation of that worship in Israel while conniving at rival gods in Judah. On the lamp left for David’s sake, Gill follows the Targum in making it a kingdom continued in his posterity; Ellicott, the victory that saved the house. Henry turns it against the heir: it aggravates the sin of a degenerate seed to fare the better for their ancestors’ piety and not imitate it.

The exception in David’s praise is read three ways. Henry calls it a remaining blot and a bar in his escutcheon, covering both the murder and the debauching of the wife, and observes that the reproach was not wiped away though the guilt was, yet the sin repented of did not throw him out of the covenant. Clarke makes it the one flagrant crime of David’s life, and not one offence but a whole system of them. Ellicott doubts it belongs to the text at all: it appears in this passage only, the Vatican and other Greek manuscripts omit it, and he suspects a marginal note that has crept in, or a comment of the compiler.

The war notice, repeated here from the previous chapter, is the harder crux. Keil and Delitzsch harmonise it by grammar, taking all the days of his life to mean so long as Abijam lived and reigned, on which reading the strangeness disappears. Gill harmonises by referent, understanding the days of Abijam rather than Rehoboam, though some, he reports, take the son to be called by his father’s name. Clarke resorts to emendation, holding the true reading to be Abijam and citing fourteen of Kennicott’s and De Rossi’s manuscripts, the Syriac, the Arabic, the Targum and the first printed Vulgate. Ellicott concedes defeat: the repetition seems inexplicable despite some artificial explanations, and probably the text is in error.
9:
The same woman is named as mother of two successive kings, and the witnesses agree how to take it. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) deny that it can mean a man had his own mother to wife, note that Thenius finds that sense and builds emendations upon it, and hold instead, with Ephraem Syrus and the Rabbins, that she kept the standing of queen-mother through the next reign until deposed for idolatry — probably because the new king’s own mother had died young. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) says the same; Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) explains the title by her having had the educating of him in childhood, and Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) cites Calmet for the usage by which Scripture calls granddaughter and daughter alike. John Gill (reformed) and Henry both treat the forty-one years as the blessing of a good king, Henry observing that the good reigns in Judah were generally the long ones, which makes the state of the church less bad than it first appears.

Gill has the consecrated persons either driven out or put to death according to the law, as many as came to the king’s knowledge, since some remained; Clarke renders the term literally as the consecrated ones; Keil and Delitzsch say he banished them. Henry marks what it cost to go further: idolatry found in the court was rooted out thence, for reformation must begin at home, and bad practices are never suppressed in the country while supported at court. He presses the difficulty, that the offender was his own grandmother — yet he loved God better, and like the Levite forgot the relation when it came into competition with his duty.

What her idol was is the chapter’s sharpest disagreement, and turns on a word found only here and in its parallel. Clarke collates six renderings — Vulgate, Greek, Syriac, Chaldee, Arabic and Jarchi — and concludes that the thing was an obscene emblem and that she held an assembly in the grove where it stood. Ellicott agrees by another road: the word seems to mean a horrible abomination of some monstrous kind, the phrase rendered in a grove should be for an asherah, and what replaced the ordinary wooden emblem was of the sort often attached to nature-worship. Keil and Delitzsch reject that outright: the word means formido, an idol as an object of fear, not a shameful image, which is how Movers explains it after the Rabbins. Henry stays with the act: the thing was publicly exposed, defaced and burnt by the brook Kidron, and she was deposed and confined to a private life.

That the high places stood is the blemish, and four accounts are given of it. Gill takes them for sites used in God’s worship before the temple was built, which the king may have thought still lawful, or which the people’s attachment made dangerous to touch. Clarke says he could not make a thorough reformation, that being left to his son, and reports Jarchi’s view that those left standing were raised by individuals for the worship of Jehovah. Ellicott finds in Chronicles an attempt at the reform that failed, the craving for local and visible sanctuaries proving too much for even earnest reformers. Henry allows that the king removed every rival image but left the altars, being loth to disoblige the people, then argues against him that they were contrary to the law, lessened men’s esteem of the temple, and stood open as a gap for idolatry — yet concludes that a heart may be perfect with God, meaning sincere rather than sinless, while falling short of good it might have done. On the dedicated things, Gill and Clarke take them for spoils his father had vowed but not lived to render, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch adding the king’s own from the Cushite war.
16:
The dating of the invasion is contradictory, the parallel account putting it in the thirty-sixth year of a king whose adversary was dead by his twenty-seventh, and four remedies are offered. John Gill (reformed) counts the thirty-six from the division of the kingdom rather than the accession — seventeen years under Rehoboam, three under Abijam — bringing the invasion to Asa’s sixteenth year, following the Jewish chronology. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) reach the same year from the Chronicles sequence: ten years of rest, the Cushite invasion in the eleventh, the thanksgiving in the fifteenth, and this in the next. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) takes the standing phrase about war to mean only that the old hostile relations continued, open war not breaking out until after the victory over Zerah. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) leaves it open: either the chronologers’ reckoning must be adopted, or there is a mistake in some of the numbers, most likely in the parallel places, which he says we have no means of correcting.

On the fortress the comment is topographical and strategic. Clarke notes that the name means a high place and takes it for a hill commanding the defile through which the chief road to Jerusalem ran, fortified to stop all intercourse lest the northern subjects cleave to David’s house. Ellicott puts it five miles north of the capital, identifies it with a village standing there still, and compares the move to the fortifying of Decelea near Athens in the Peloponnesian war, a standing menace beside a hostile capital; he adds that a chief who had seen earlier invasions fail might prefer this easier way of keeping the enemy in check, and connects the blockade with the falling away of many from Israel to Judah.

The alliance bought with temple treasure is condemned by all, on different counts. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) lists three: that the king tempted Benhadad to break a league and violate the public faith; that he could not trust the God who had already delivered him; and that he took gold from a treasury not to be touched save on extraordinary occasions. Clarke is harsher about the motive: no danger threatened which the king could not have turned aside himself, so he probably meant to destroy the northern kingdom outright and robbed the house of the Lord to do it. Ellicott weighs policy and faith together: it was the first calling in of a heathen power against his brethren the children of Israel, a desperate expedient and an unfaithfulness to a brotherhood separation had not dissolved, and it earned the rebuke it received — as Isaiah afterwards denounced trust in confederacies. Keil and Delitzsch mark the inconsistency: the king who sought the Lord’s help against the Cushites sought Syrian help against Israel.

The stratagem worked. Keil and Delitzsch have the Syrian captains take the northern cities and compel Baasha to abandon the building and withdraw to his capital, locating the two places afterwards fortified from the spoil; Ellicott observes that the king pushed his own works further north. Clarke draws a maxim from the levy no man was exempted from: where boundaries must be fortified against an enemy, all exemptions cease. Henry grants that the design prospered and yet displeased God, the king being told by the prophet that he had done foolishly and should thenceforth have wars. On the disease of his old age Clarke calls it a rheumatic affection or the gout, three years before the death, and notes with the others that he sought the physicians and not the Lord — Keil and Delitzsch inferring that the longer he lived the further his heart turned away, Ellicott adding that he imprisoned the seer who rebuked him, prosperity having told on a character still faithful in worship. Henry says only that the gout made him peevish with those about him.
25:
The northern kingdom’s instability frames the closing section. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) counts six or seven hands holding the government during the single reign of Asa — Jeroboam at the beginning and Ahab at the end, with Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Tibni and Omri undermining and destroying one another between — and takes it for the fulfilment of the threat that they should be as a reed shaken in the water, got by deserting the house both of God and of David. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reaches the same contrast from the other side: Baasha is the first of the many military chiefs who seized the throne of Israel by violence or assassination, and the constant succession of ephemeral dynasties stands against the unchanged royalty of David’s house, resting on the promise of God. On the son who was killed Henry notes a chance thrown away, since a brother’s death might have made him religious; Ellicott takes the recurring formula about doing evil to mean perseverance in the system Jeroboam introduced.

The siege is placed and judged. Henry has the town one the Philistines had taken from the Danites; Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls it a city of Dan generally in Philistine hands; Ellicott makes it a Levitical town probably never recovered until David subdued the Philistines, reads in the text a Philistine revolt against the enfeebled power of Israel, notes that the place commanded a pass from the plain of Sharon inland, and observes that the siege must have been fruitless of lasting result, since twenty-six years later the town is still in enemy hands. Henry adds the detail that condemns the murdered king more than the murder does: so little interest had he in the affections of his people that his army not only did not avenge his death but chose his murderer to succeed him.

Why the conspirator struck is left open or settled according to the witness. Henry will not decide between personal pique, revenge for some affront, a pretence of freeing the country from a bad prince, and plain ambition. John Gill (reformed) guesses an officer of the army whose chief view was the kingdom, and Ellicott agrees that no motive but ambition need be supposed, denying any formal commission of vengeance — which he infers from the later declaration that judgment fell on him in part for the killing itself. From that he draws the sentence that carries the paragraph: sin which works out God’s purpose is not the less truly sin. Clarke puts the providence flatly, that God made use of one wicked man to destroy another, and Gill turns it against the executioner, who destroyed the family not from any dislike of Jeroboam’s sins, since he walked in them himself, but because the Lord had threatened it.

On the reign that followed, the comment is on its sameness. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) note that the prophet’s words against this house coincide exactly, with the necessary changes, with those against Jeroboam’s, and remark on the strange perversity of kings who had seen the families before them overthrown for the calf-worship, had overturned those families themselves, and then worshipped the same calves. Clarke draws the same lesson as a rule: the entail of iniquity cannot be cut off but by a thorough conversion of the soul to God, of which these kings seem to have had no adequate notion, so that the wicked followed the steps of the wicked and grew worse, sin gathering strength by exercise and age. Gill observes that the whole kingdom submitted to a usurper and murderer, and accounts for the standing hostility with Judah by the impossibility of any good understanding between them. Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke both note that the notice of that war is simply a repetition of what the chapter has already said.
